title: Presentation
text:
We invite all SoG PGRs in their second, third and fourth years the opportunity to present a research talk. This could be an aspect of your PhD thesis, or a research project/paper that you have contributed to. Presentations should be 9 minutes, followed by 3 minutes of Q&A.

Guidelines for Presenting

The presentation must be 9 minutes, so please keep to the timings. It will be great practice for future conferences that might be a bit more strict!
Audience will have the opportunity to ask questions to the presenter for 3 minutes, directly after the presentation.
The session chair will help manage time, notifying when there are a few minutes left and coordinating the following Q/A.
Any PowerPoint presentations must be submitted through this form by October 25th.
Enjoy the experience! The PGR conference will be a relaxed and positive environment. It will be a great opportunity to practice your presentation skills and test out your ideas.

title: Lightning Talk
text:
We invite all first-year PGRs and MRES students an opportunity to present a lightning talk: your presentation should last around 3 minutes, and will be followed by 2 minutes of Q&A. This could be a brief introduction to yourself or some initial research ideas! The floor is yours, and it’s a great opportunity to introduce yourself to your peers in a fun, relaxed setting.
If you would like to use some slides or a visual background (this is optional), please submit them through this form by October 25th.

title: Awards
text: The organising committee will distribute awards for Best Full Talk (year 2+) and Best Lightning Talk (year 1). Each winner will receive a gift voucher.

title: School of Geography PGR Conference 2026
text:
Welcome to the School of Geography PGR Conference at the University of Leeds. The conference will take place on the 2nd November 2026, and is open to all PGRs and academic staff here at the School of Geography!
The PGR conference has been a longstanding event within the School of Geography to showcase the exciting and important research from postgraduates. The conference provides an opportunity for postgraduates to present ongoing research, network with peers and develop new insights in a friendly and constructive setting. It is expected that all postgraduates from across the School of Geography attend.
The School of Geography PGR conference will include:

9-min presentations from years 2, 3 and 4 PGRs followed by 3-min Q&A
First year PGR and MRES lightning talk sessions
Lunch & Social – Snacks, Board Games and Table Tennis at Crossroads (Level -1 of Leeds University Union)

Lunch will be provided - however please bring your own water bottle + mug for refreshments!

title: Presenters
text:
Title: Impact of windfarms on peatland carbon cycle processes



Title: Large language models for localised climate solutions: What can AI language models tell us about how textual information influences understanding of environmental issues?
Abstract: Place-based climate action has emerged as a key method for the delivery of effective and context-specific responses to challenges at the local and regional levels. However, meaningful action depends heavily on access to reliable, expert knowledge presented in a format that is understandable and actionable for non-specialists, grounded in the local context.
Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise as a method to deliver complex climate information in an accessible format, however, their effectiveness in local climate contexts is limited by possible hallucination and a lack of access to place-specific information. They have also not been tested yet in real-word context to evaluate their effectiveness in assisting local climate action. To address this, we propose a retrieval augmented (RAG) LLM assistant that integrates various local and national documents and policies with scientific reports to provide climate information that is grounded in local context.
After technical evaluation, the assistant was tested in the context of a mini‑public on local climate action in Kirklees. Participants were asked to use the assistant as a source of information during the session to inform the creation of local climate‑related proposals, which were then forwarded to the local council for assessment. This process and the resulting proposals were compared against those produced by a control group operating without access to the assistant. Initial analysis suggests that retrieval‑based grounding improves the local relevance and interpretability of generated outputs and supports the development of more actionable proposals suitable for implementation by community groups or local councils.



Title: From Cognitive Distance to Accessibility in Cities: Individuals, Places, and Time
Abstract: Classic calculated measures of urban accessibility, based solely on transportation and land use metrics, are not enough to adequately explain individual’s behaviour in cities. An individual can only act based on their personal understanding of said environment, which in reality can be biased, distorted and incomplete in a variety of ways. Perceived accessibility aims to fill that gap, explicitly positioning one’s perception of access as the quantity to be measured. This field, however, has so far relied only on survey measurements, with very limited inquiry into the cognitive processes that shape the perceived environment and what causes the differences between the physical and perceived to emerge.
At the same time, scholars in spatial cognition have spent decades trying to understand these processes, from the first conceptualizations of the brain as a black box, stimulus-response system to theories of embodied cognition and external representations. While numerous authors in the past have proposed a series of factors that may influence the perception of distances between places, these have never been synthesized into one cohesive model, nor have they been more widely considered in urban and transportation planning.
This project aims to bridge those gaps. Understanding how different individuals understand distance differently, how the distribution of places in space is conceptualized, and how this varies through time will allow for the creation of new metrics of accessibility that explicitly consider how distances between unseen places are actually felt, and what implications this may bring to urban planning.



Title: Urban Redevelopment for whom? Developing practice-based knowledge for inclusive market redevelopment schemes in the UK
Abstract: My research explores the redevelopment of traditional retail markets in the UK and is interdisciplinary in nature as it draws from multiple disciplines - critical geography, urban studies, architecture, and sociology to explore how traditional markets acts as social public spaces. These traditional markets have been important spaces within the local economy providing affordable and culturally diverse food and drink options to migrant populations, low-income communities, ethnic minority groups, and the elderly in the UK. However, they are facing increasing pressures of gentrification which risk these vulnerable communities and their access to affordable food and other goods and services. These markets are often transformed into gourmet markets post redevelopment catering to higher-income groups. This gourmetisation of food reflects a class and race-based process wherein a segment of Western societies imposes narrow definitions of what constitutes ‘healthy’ food, often with limited tolerance for the cultural food practices of marginalized and migrant groups. The research also aims to explore how social relationships among traders, customers, local authorities, market managers, architects and campaign groups are reshaped during redevelopment processes, paying particular attention to the power dynamics that influence whose voices, interests, and forms of knowledge are prioritised in decision-making. This research explores the diverse rhythms of the market, including traders setting up the market stall, customer engagement, informal conversations, variations in activity across the day and the process of market closure and moving to the temporary market site. Ultimately, the project aims that future market redevelopment schemes support existing marginalised communities rather than contribute to their exclusion or displacement.

title: Presenters
text:
Session 2:

Anna Ray, EGC
Title: Climate Change and Microbial Carbon Cycling in Tropical Forest Soils
Abstract: Tropical forests are crucial for regulating the Earth’s climate, playing a key role in global carbon (C) cycling through atmospheric Carbon Dioxide (CO₂) exchange. The interactive impacts of higher temperatures and changes to precipitation patterns due to climatic change could substantially alter microbially mediated CO₂ emissions from tropical forest soils.
The presentation will discuss field observations showing CO₂ response from tropical forest soils after 9 years of experimental warming (+3 °C) (Barro Colorado Island, Panama). Preliminary findings indicate for every 1°C increase in soil temperature compared to ambient, CO₂ efflux increases by about 0.76 μmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹. Temporal variation of this effect was evident, with higher emissions from June – September (wet season) but not during the dry season suggesting an important temperature and moisture interaction.
Laboratory incubations were informed by field-observed CO₂ response and used to examine the microbial mechanisms underlying the warming effects. Interactions of microbial physiological response were later evaluated through assessing microbial activity, substrate availability and extracellular enzyme activity (EEA), but are beyond the scope of this presentation.
Linking field observations with mechanistic investigations, this research aims to improve our understanding of the processes driving tropical soil C responses to climate change and to provide evidence for improving representation of tropical soil processes in Earth System Models.


Claudia Alvarado, RBPM
Title: (HI-RISE) Himalayan glacier-fed river and stream ecology: The extent to which macroinvertebrate and algal community structure and function is influenced by catchment glaciality in a monsoon-dominated climate
Abstract: Himalayan glacier-fed streams are critically understudied, and the potential impact of projected warming and future glacier loss on constituent ecosystems is unknown. Results from other alpine regions cannot be easily extrapolated to Himalayan contexts, where streams are subject to stronger forcings (in terms of relative altitude, temperature, oxygen limitation, UV exposure and unique monsoon influence) and may host rare and cryptic endemics. This research explores the relationship between glacier indices, hydrochemical variables, and stream ecology community metrics described in existing studies from the Himalayan region and derived from in depth sampling of 20 streams in Sagarmatha National Park, Nepal (spanning 3300-4800m altitude and 0%-74% catchment glacier cover) in April and October 2025. The research will investigate macroinvertebrate and algal community responses in particular, aiming to highlight the implications of these responses on ecosystem functioning, wider food webs and human water users.


Bhagya Sri Chintakula, ISDS
Title: Identifying Priority Places for Increasing Physical Activity in UK


Frank Chen, ISDS
Title: Understanding the relationship between food behaviour and health outcomes
Abstract: Supermarket transaction data offer new opportunities to understand food purchasing behaviours and their relationships with population health. However, translating these records into meaningful measures of dietary exposure remains challenging due to temporal variability, population heterogeneity and the geographical mismatch between shopping and residential locations. This research develops a framework for using transaction data to estimate habitual food purchasing patterns and their associations with health outcomes at small-area levels. It first examines the temporal stability of purchasing behaviours and the observation periods required to identify habitual patterns. Spatial interaction modelling and geodemographic calibration are then used to account for cross-boundary shopping and differences between shoppers and resident populations. Finally, purchasing measures are calibrated against dietary intake data and linked to local health indicators. By addressing the temporal, spatial and population representativeness of transaction data, this research aims to strengthen their application in nutritional epidemiology and place-based public health research.


Ode Zulkarnain Sahji Tihurua, SJCC
Title: When is a Plantation a Ruin? Colonial Afterlives and the Uneven Postcolonial Landscape
Abstract: When does a colonial plantation become a ruin? This question prompts a consideration of dominant understandings of colonial ruins as discrete, bounded remnants of the colonial past. Drawing on preliminary ethnographic work conducted in August 2026 in the Banda Islands, Indonesia, this article traces how the material, ecological, social, and institutional components that once constituted the colonial nutmeg plantation system followed divergent trajectories after the end of colonial rule. I develop the concept of ‘differential afterlives’ to describe how the heterogeneous components of a plantation formation persist, decay, adapt, or disappear according to distinct yet interconnected temporal trajectories. The varied conditions found across different sites demonstrate that colonial plantations did not become ruins simultaneously or as a coherent whole. The buildings, groves, nutmeg trees, production spaces, labour practices, social relations, and institutions that once formed the plantation persisted, decayed, grew, were repurposed, or were reconfigured through distinct temporalities. By shifting the focus from ruins as material objects to the differential processes through which plantation relations persist and transform, the article argues that ruination must be understood as a relational and uneven process. From this perspective, plantation ruins are not merely material evidence of a bygone colonial era but active components of the processes that continuously shape the postcolonial landscape of the Banda Islands.

Session 3:

Rossana Escanilla-Minchel, RBPM
Title: Hydrological Responses to Climate and Land-Cover Change in Central Chile


Yasmin Belhadj, SJCC
Title: Occupying space: surveillance and protest in UK universities
Abstract: Since 2020, student activist movements have re-emerged within UK universities, coinciding with the growing criminalisation of protest. Parallel to this surge, many universities have acted as an extension of state control, responding to student protest with securitisation measures through the extensive use of surveillance apparatus and academic punishment. This project focuses on this phenomenon, investigating the ways in which universities have engaged with and reacted to student protest groups during 2020-2025. First, it examines how securitisation has become normalised within universities as a response to protest. Second, it explores how universities use surveillance and its coercive effects on student protestors. Finally, it examines how universities use negotiation tactics and bureaucracy to demobilise protest.
This research contributes to existing scholarship on protest repression in the UK, focusing on three recent sites of struggle within universities. This project helps disseminate the knowledge and experiences of people facing violence and criminalisation within universities. Drawing from militant ethnographies, anarchist methodologies and scholar-activism, this thesis analyses fourteen semi-structured interviews of student activists from three anonymised UK universities. Freedom of Information requests were also used to collect data on campus security budgets and relationships to the police and armed forces.
The findings from this study show that universities perceive protest as a threat to their campuses and have constructed narratives of crisis to delegitimise protest. While the universities are not as well equipped at surveillance as the police, they do have the surveillance capabilities to punish student protestors and often emulate their aesthetics through their uniforms and mannerisms. The findings also indicate that the universities in practice lack competence at surveillance, and that the idea of the university as a panoptic institution may be more effective at deterring protest.


Jade Parker, ISDS
Title: Community Sentence Requirements and the Construction of Reoffending


Keval Dodhia, EGC
Title: Using novel hydraulic traits to determine hydraulic function of tropical trees through mechanistic modelling
Abstract: Southern Amazon forests are among the driest, and most seasonal forests in the Amazon. Projected climate change is expected to increase stress on these forests. Observed temperatures and VPD are rising, drought frequency increases, and dry seasons get longer. Which species will cope and which will be most at risk remains unclear.
Together these changes are expected to increase the stress on tropical tree hydraulic system (water conductance from soil to canopy) and some of the species may become vulnerable to hydraulic failure. In order to predict how hydraulic stress will affect composition of these forests a suitable tree model should be able to represent the hydraulic system of trees and its thresholds to hydraulic failure (embolisms). Thus it should predict water potentials through the plant to relate to hydraulic safety margins. Similarly the model should have a realistic representation of soil water conductance to predict soil potential profiles.
Here we profit from an ongoing drought experiment in Tanguro, Mato Grosso, in the southern Amazon with comprehensible datasets related to hydraulics to test the ability of such a model – Sperry model for the tree and Richards model for soils.
Here I show the current effectiveness of the model, set-backs, and resolutions I am working on. I show how the data is collected for modelling, the detailed data sets we must use to drive the model, and what inputs will will need in the future.

title: Presenters
text:
Session 4:

Yue Che, SJCC
Title: Rethinking the role of state-owned enterprises in Chinese urban governance: Taking the SOE jiashuyuan regeneration as an example
Abstract: Research on political-business relations in China has largely focused on the collusion between stateowned enterprises (SOEs) and local governments. However, with the growth of the private sector and ongoing urbanization, the roles of SOEs, the private sector, and local states require further exploration. This research examines the urban renewal process of a residential community built by an SOE in a small industrial city in western China, exploring the roles of state-business relations in this process. Through ethnographic fieldwork, this research reveals that SOE collaborates closely with local governments and developers, using its influence to build a connection between local states and residents, reduce conflict to ensure project progress, and use collaborative frameworks to seek their benefits. the research highlights how SOEs play a role in urban renewal, while power struggles between residents and local states impact the SOEs’ ability to gain further resources and influence, to contribute new theoretical insights into the role of state-business relations in China’s urbanization.


Arthur Lamoliere, RBPM
Title: Predicting biodiversity loss in mountain rivers due to glacier retreat


Imogen Carter, EGC
Title: Tree ring stable isotopes to infer climate and tree physiological responses to climate change
Abstract: Tree ring stable isotope ratios are powerful tools to develop precisely dated and highly resolved reconstructions of past climate as well as to provide insights into the physiological responses of trees to environmental changes. In this talk I discuss how I’m using tree ring isotopes (oxygen- δ18O, carbon- δ13C, hydrogen- δ2H) for these applications in my 2nd and 3rd thesis chapters. Last year I collected tree ring cores of ancient Montezuma Baldcypress trees from four sites in San Luis Potosí and Durango in Mexico, with the aim to assess potential climate-driven changes in their water-use efficiency. I discuss the surprising δ18O and δ13C trends since 1990 for these sites, and the implications of these pilot results for constructing a long-term tree ring chronology. I then dive into the results (and challenges!) so far for the Leverhulme project I’m a part of. The project aims to disentangle isotope signals originating from source water (reflecting large-scale climate) and from leaf water (reflecting local climate) in tree rings. This involves measuring δ18O and δ2H of tree ring constituents (lignin, cellulose, specific positions in cellulose) of tree ring samples collected across three altitudinal transects from La Palma, Hawaii and Peru. So far, we find δ18O and δ2H of tree ring cellulose reflects leaf water δ18O and δ2H trends along the altitudinal gradients, as expected. Surprisingly, δ2H of lignin shows no altitudinal trend, or reflects altitudinal changes in leaf water δ2H, in contrast to previous studies that show a strong correlation with source water δ2H across large spatial scales. I discuss possible reasons for this unexpected trend, and the exciting chemical methods I’m working on at the moment for the other isotope measurements.


Paddy Smith, ISDS
Title: Hierarchical Structures and Anchors within Online Place Descriptions

title: Presenters
text:
Session 5:

Sanola Sandiford, EGC
Title: Future Climate Impacts on Travel for Arctic Communities
Abstract: Greenland is undergoing significant environmental transformation due to climate change, with implications for travel and transportation networks. Informal ice, sea and land routes (referred to here as ‘trails’) that Inuit communities regularly traverse are particularly vulnerable to changing environmental conditions. These trails connect towns and settlements, support hunting and fishing, and enable access to important cultural sites. Changes to these trails may make travel increasingly challenging, particularly for remote communities. Understanding how climate change may affect trail accessibility is therefore important for anticipating future changes in mobility and developing adaptation strategies. This research investigates future climate change impacts on trail accessibility around Qeqertarsuaq, in the Disko Bay region of northwest Greenland, by integrating climate model projections and Indigenous Knowledge. Semi-structured interviews with community members identified locally relevant environmental thresholds related to wind, sea ice, temperature and precipitation that influence whether specific trails can be travelled safely. These thresholds will be combined with climate projections to develop trail-access models that estimate when different routes may become inaccessible over the coming century. This provides an interdisciplinary framework for examining future climate impacts on Arctic trail mobility and demonstrates how different knowledge systems can be combined to support locally relevant adaptation planning.


Akhil Javad, EGC
Title: Accelerated Growth in Regenerating Boreal Forests


Tom Smith, RBPM
Title: Hydrologically Informed Estimates of Malaria Transmission
Abstract: Malaria vector and parasite life cycles are climate-sensitive; they depend on temperature and surface water availability. As such the suitability of a given climate to malaria can be estimated through process-based modelling. The effect of temperature in such process-based models is well constrained by empirically derived thermal response curves. Yet, the availability of surface water, until recently, was crudely approximated using precipitation thresholds, ignoring the key hydrological processes that determine the distribution of surface water. Here we seek to extend current modelling efforts incorporating basic hydrological understanding into continental-scale estimates of malaria risk. Many studies look forward in time and project future changes in malaria risk, contrastingly we look backwards to attribute changes in malaria risk that have already occurred to anthropogenic climate forcings. This research asks: How does malaria risk in our world differ from a world in which climate change did not occur?


Hannah Barnett, RBPM
Title: A new global database of water availability to glaciers
Abstract: TBC


Prahelika Deka, SJCC
Title: (Re)Imagining climate futures: An ethnographic and creative exploration of futuremaking in Majuli Island, India
Abstract: This project investigates the alternative, possible imagined futures of Majuli Island in Assam, India, based on people’s social and temporal imaginaries. In the face of a rapidly changing climate and increasing reporting of floods and erosion, popular narratives of the island depict a dystopian future of complete submergence of the island. While dominant climate narratives portray Majuli’s doomed future, this thesis argues that residents already inhabit multiple, competing futures that challenge this singular dystopian imaginary. Within such a scenario, this study examines how people imagine their futures as well as their island/river’s futures and how intersecting social identities such as spiritual and everyday beliefs, age and gender influence their imagination.
Using participant-led, creative methodologies, I respond to the emerging notion of an imagination crisis in climate change research. In doing so, I also engage with emerging literature on imagination, futures and plurality of waters and examine the everyday ways of life, the relationships people share with their land/river and the emotions that drive the meaning-making of both space and time. I argue there is not a lack of imagination but the failure in identifying and/or accommodating multiple alternate imagined futures from dominant climate imaginaries. This research is therefore significant and timely in addressing the frontline climate survivors’ visions in Majuli and similar areas in the public and non-public discourses.
